narrative:
The model predicted an 80% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to decide on law school entry, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. Your undergraduate GPA ranked third and added further weight in the same direction.

Compared with students who were accepted, you finished both your first and third years in a much lower decile (2 versus averages around 6 and 5.8). Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 also sat noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students. These academic performance signals were the main reasons the model saw a high risk of bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score of 36 was only slightly below the accepted average of 37.2, your middle family income is fairly common among accepted applicants, and you plan to attend full-time, which is the norm. None of these moved the prediction much.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance if you retake courses or enroll in a post-baccalaureate program, and consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score. Stronger grades and test results in a future application would likely change the model’s outlook. (218 words)
